items.stem: A reaction transfers energy to the surroundings. What must be true of the product molecules?

options.text: They have less energy than the reactants, by the amount transferred out.
They have more energy than the reactants, by the amount given out.
They have less energy, and the energy released no longer exists.
They have exactly the same total energy as the reactants did.

items.why: This is the specification's own statement: the energy that reached the surroundings came from the chemicals, so the products sit lower by exactly that amount.

items.stem: Which statement about energy during a chemical reaction is correct?

options.text: No energy is transferred to or from the surroundings at all.
The total energy in the universe is the same after the reaction as before.
Some of the energy is destroyed as the surroundings are being warmed.
Reactants and products always contain exactly equal energy.

items.why: Energy is conserved in chemical reactions; the reaction only moves energy between the chemicals and their surroundings.

items.stem: Which statement describes an exothermic reaction?

options.text: It takes in energy from the surroundings, so their temperature rises.
It transfers energy out, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
It transfers energy to the surroundings, so their temperature rises.
It stores the energy inside the products, so nothing warms up.

items.why: This is the specification definition: energy goes out to the surroundings and the temperature of the surroundings increases.

items.stem: Which of these reactions is exothermic?

options.text: the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate
the reaction inside a sports injury cold pack
citric acid reacting with sodium hydrogencarbonate
the neutralisation of an acid by an alkali

items.why: Neutralisation is one of the three exothermic examples named by the specification, alongside combustion and many oxidation reactions.

items.stem: Magnesium ribbon is lit with a Bunsen flame and burns brightly, warming the tripod above it. Why is this reaction described as exothermic?

options.text: Energy had to be supplied by the flame, so energy is taken in overall here.
Combustion transfers energy to the surroundings, and that is why the tripod warms.
The oxidation takes in energy from the surrounding air, making it glow.
Burning stores the energy in the magnesium oxide that is produced.

items.why: Combustion is exothermic; the flame only starts it, and the energy warming the tripod comes out of the chemicals.

items.stem: A hand warmer contains iron powder that oxidises slowly once the pack is opened. Why does the pack become warm?

options.text: The pack takes energy in from your own hand, and this is what makes it warm.
The reaction is endothermic, so it lets out the heat it had stored.
The oxidation is exothermic and transfers energy to your hands and the air.
Slow reactions give out no energy; the padding keeps hands warm.

items.why: Many oxidation reactions are exothermic, and the specification names hand warmers as an everyday use of one.

items.stem: Which statement describes an endothermic reaction?

options.text: It takes in energy from the surroundings, so their temperature will rise.
It gives out energy, and so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
It releases the energy that was stored inside the reactants.
It takes energy in from the surroundings, so their temperature falls.

items.why: This is the specification definition: energy is taken in from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.

items.stem: Copper carbonate is heated strongly and breaks down into copper oxide and carbon dioxide. Why is this reaction endothermic?

options.text: Energy is taken in to break the compound down.
Energy is given out because a hot flame is used here.
Energy is stored, then released as the gas escapes.
Energy is destroyed as the carbonate breaks apart.

items.why: Thermal decompositions are endothermic: energy has to be supplied continuously from the surroundings for the compound to break down.

items.stem: Citric acid solution is stirred with sodium hydrogencarbonate. The mixture fizzes and the thermometer falls from 21 °C to 15 °C. What does this show?

options.text: The reaction is exothermic, as the fizzing shows energy leaving.
The reaction is exothermic, since the chemicals have lost energy.
The reaction is endothermic and takes energy in from the surroundings.
No energy was transferred, as 6 °C is too small a change.

items.why: The temperature of the surroundings has decreased, which is the specification's test for an endothermic reaction; this pair is its named example.

items.stem: A student measures the temperature of the surroundings before and after four reactions. Which result shows an endothermic reaction?

options.text: The temperature rose from 22.0 °C to 31.5 °C during this reaction.
The temperature rose from 16.5 °C to 22.0 °C as it went along.
The temperature stayed at 22.0 °C throughout the reaction.
The temperature fell from 22.0 °C to 16.5 °C during the reaction.

items.why: A fall in the temperature of the surroundings is exactly how the specification says an endothermic reaction is recognised.

items.stem: During a neutralisation the thermometer in the mixture rises by 8 °C. What has happened to the energy?

options.text: It has been transferred from the chemicals to the surroundings.
It has been transferred from the surroundings and into the chemicals.
The chemicals still hold the very same energy they had before.
It has been stored in the salt and the water that are made.

items.why: The solution is part of the surroundings, so a rise in its temperature shows energy leaving the chemicals: an exothermic reaction.

items.stem: A sports injury pack and a hand warmer each rely on a chemical reaction. Which comparison is correct?

options.text: The injury pack is exothermic; the hand warmer is endothermic.
The injury pack is endothermic and the warmer exothermic.
Both are exothermic, but the injury pack releases energy slowly.
Both are endothermic, and each takes energy from the skin.

items.why: The pack must take energy in from the surroundings to cool a swelling, while the warmer must transfer energy out to the hands.

items.stem: A self-heating can warms coffee using the reaction of calcium oxide with water. Which property makes this reaction suitable for that use?

options.text: It is endothermic, so it draws energy out of the air and into the drink.
It is exothermic, so the reacting chemicals themselves become hotter.
It is exothermic, but only when the temperature change is large.
It is exothermic, so it transfers enough energy to warm the drink in the can.

items.why: An everyday use of an exothermic reaction: energy released by the reaction passes into the drink and raises its temperature.

items.stem: In Required practical 4 a student adds different volumes of sodium hydroxide to 25 cm3 of acid and records the highest temperature reached. What is the independent variable?

options.text: the volume of sodium hydroxide added
the highest temperature that is reached
the temperature of the acid before mixing
the insulation of the plastic cup

items.why: It is the variable the student deliberately chooses and changes; the highest temperature is what is measured as a result.

items.stem: Why is the reacting mixture in Required practical 4 placed in a polystyrene cup with a lid?

options.text: to make the reaction happen faster inside the insulated cup
to reduce the energy transferred to and from the surroundings
to make the reaction go faster so that a change can be seen sooner
to stop the temperature of the room from changing at all

items.why: Polystyrene insulates and the lid limits evaporation, so more of the energy change shows up as a temperature change in the mixture.

items.stem: Two reactant particles collide with each other but no reaction takes place. What is the reason?

options.text: Every collision must react, so this cannot happen.
They collided with less than the energy given out here.
They collided with too little energy to react.
The reaction is exothermic, so no energy is needed.

items.why: Reactions occur only when particles collide with sufficient energy; a collision below the activation energy simply bounces apart.

items.stem: What is meant by the activation energy of a reaction?

options.text: the minimum amount of energy that particles must have in order to react
the height of the peak measured from the bottom axis of the diagram
the total amount of energy the reaction gives out overall
the energy released whenever two reactant particles collide

items.why: This is the specification's definition of the activation energy, word for word in substance.

items.stem: Which set of quantities can be shown on a reaction profile?

options.text: the temperature change, provided it is large enough to count as a real energy transfer
the relative energies of the reactants and products, the activation energy and the overall energy change
the activation energy on its own, because the products are not marked anywhere on the diagram
the rise in temperature, showing the energy that the chemicals have taken in

items.why: These are precisely the three things the specification says a reaction profile can be used to show.

items.stem: A student draws a reaction profile for an endothermic reaction. Which description of the drawing is correct?

options.text: The products line lies below the reactants, joined by a curve with a peak.
A straight sloping line runs from the reactants line up to the products.
The products line lies above the reactants, joined by a curved peak.
The top of the curve is level with the products line on the right.

items.why: Endothermic products are higher in energy than the reactants, and the specification asks for a curved line passing over the activation energy peak.

items.stem: A reaction profile shows the products at a lower energy than the reactants. What does this tell you about the reaction?

options.text: It is endothermic and takes in energy overall.
It is exothermic only if the peak is low.
It cannot happen, as products must be higher.
It is exothermic and gives out energy.

items.why: Products lower than reactants means the chemicals have lost energy, and that energy has gone to the surroundings.

items.stem: Why must colliding particles have at least the activation energy?

options.text: because it is the energy the reaction gives to the surroundings
because it is the energy that is needed for the reaction to occur
because it is only needed when a reaction is endothermic
because it is the energy needed to make particles collide

items.why: The specification puts it in exactly these terms: the activation energy is the energy needed for a reaction to occur.

items.stem: During a chemical reaction, what happens to the bonds in the reactants?

options.text: Energy is released as each one of them breaks.
They break with no energy change at all.
Energy must be supplied so that they break.
They break, and forming new bonds also takes energy.

items.why: The specification states that energy must be supplied to break bonds in the reactants, so bond breaking takes energy in.

items.stem: What happens to energy when the bonds in the products are formed?

options.text: Energy is released only if it is exothermic.
Energy must be supplied to make them form.
Energy is stored and none gets out.
Energy is released as these bonds form.

items.why: The specification states that energy is released when bonds in the products are formed.

items.stem: A student is given a table of bond energies for a reaction. What can these values be used to calculate?

options.text: the energy taken in breaking bonds and released forming them
the total energy of the reaction, by adding up every value in the table
the number of bonds broken and the number of bonds formed in total
the temperature rise, showing the energy the chemicals take in

items.why: Bond energies give both sums the specification names: the energy needed to break bonds and the energy released when bonds are formed.

items.stem: How is the overall energy change of a reaction found from bond energies?

options.text: the sum of the energy released forming bonds minus the sum needed to break
the sum of the energy needed to break bonds added to the sum released
the sum of the energy needed to break bonds minus the sum released forming bonds
the number of bonds broken subtracted from the number of bonds made

items.why: This is the specification's definition of the overall energy change: the difference between the two sums, taken in that order.

items.stem: H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl. Bond energies in kJ/mol: H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431. What is the overall energy change?

options.text: +1540 kJ/mol, adding all the values up
+184 kJ/mol, so it is endothermic
+247 kJ/mol, using one H-Cl bond
-184 kJ/mol, so this is exothermic

items.why: Breaking: 436 + 242 = 678. Forming: 2 x 431 = 862. Overall energy change = 678 - 862 = -184 kJ/mol, so energy is given out.

items.stem: In an exothermic reaction, how do the two bond energy sums compare?

options.text: Forming new bonds releases more than breaking bonds needs.
Breaking existing bonds needs more than forming new bonds gives out.
More bonds are formed in the products than are broken overall.
The two sums are equal, so no energy is left over here.

items.why: The specification states that in an exothermic reaction the energy released from forming new bonds is greater than the energy needed to break existing bonds.

items.stem: A reaction is endothermic. What does this tell you about the bond energy sums?

options.text: More bonds are broken than are formed in this reaction.
Breaking bonds needs more than forming lets out.
Forming bonds gives out more than breaking needs.
Forming new bonds takes in energy, making it endothermic.

items.why: The specification states that in an endothermic reaction the energy needed to break existing bonds is greater than the energy released from forming new bonds.

items.stem: A chemical cell is connected to a lamp and the lamp lights. Where does the electricity come from?

options.text: From chemicals inside the cell that react together
From electricity stored in the cell already
From a store of electrons in the metal casing
From energy stored inside it, like a battery

items.why: Cells contain chemicals which react to produce electricity; the reaction runs only once the circuit is complete.

items.stem: Two cells are identical except that one uses zinc and copper electrodes and the other uses magnesium and copper. The cells give different voltages. Why?

options.text: The voltage depends on how much electrolyte there is
The voltage depends on the type of electrode used
The voltage depends on the area of the electrode
The voltage depends on the wire joining them up

items.why: The voltage produced by a cell depends on a number of factors, including the type of electrode.

items.stem: A simple cell uses zinc and copper electrodes in copper sulfate solution. The copper sulfate solution is replaced by a different electrolyte, with everything else unchanged. What happens to the voltage?

options.text: It stays the same, because only the metals matter here
It stays the same for any liquid, even for pure water
It may change, as the voltage depends on electrolyte
It changes only if the new electrolyte is an acid

items.why: The voltage produced by a cell depends on the type of electrolyte as well as the type of electrode.

items.stem: Which pair of electrodes, dipped into an electrolyte, would produce a voltage?

options.text: Two identical strips of copper metal
Two copper strips of different size
Two carbon rods taken from cells
A zinc strip and a copper strip

items.why: A simple cell is made by connecting two different metals in contact with an electrolyte.

items.stem: A battery is made by connecting four 1.5 V cells together in series. What voltage does the battery provide, and why?

options.text: 1.5 V, because the cells share one voltage
6.0 V, because the voltages of the cells add up
6.0 V, because the current from each cell adds
0.375 V, as the voltage is split between them

items.why: Batteries consist of two or more cells connected in series to provide a greater voltage.

items.stem: A non-rechargeable cell stops producing a voltage after some time in use. Why does it stop?

options.text: All the electrons inside the cell have been used up
The electrolyte has leaked out of its case
One of the reactants has been completely used up
Both of the electrodes have been fully used up

items.why: In non-rechargeable cells the chemical reactions stop when one of the reactants has been used up.

items.stem: Which statement about alkaline batteries is correct?

options.text: They can be recharged from the mains many times over
They are rechargeable once the alkali is replaced
They work again once fresh reactants are added
They are non-rechargeable, so they are replaced

items.why: The specification states that alkaline batteries are non-rechargeable.

items.stem: A rechargeable cell is connected to an external electrical supply. What happens inside the cell?

options.text: The chemical reactions are reversed
Fresh reactants are pushed into the cell
Extra electrons are stored inside it
The used-up reactants are all removed

items.why: Rechargeable cells can be recharged because the chemical reactions are reversed when an external current is supplied.

items.stem: Cells are made from a copper electrode and one other metal in the same electrolyte. The voltages are: magnesium 2.7 V, zinc 1.1 V, iron 0.8 V. Tin is less reactive than iron but more reactive than copper. What voltage would a tin and copper cell most likely give?

options.text: About 1.9 V, from the zinc and iron values added
About 3.4 V, since tin is the least reactive metal
About 0.5 V, because tin is close to copper in reactivity
About 2.7 V, the same as the magnesium cell gives

items.why: The voltage rises with the difference in reactivity, so tin, just above copper, gives a small voltage.

items.stem: Where does the hydrogen in a hydrogen fuel cell come from?

options.text: It is stored inside the cell when the cell is built
It is made inside the cell from air and water
It is released by the electrolyte as it runs
It is fed in from an external supply of the fuel

items.why: Fuel cells are supplied by an external source of fuel (eg hydrogen) and oxygen or air.

items.stem: In a hydrogen fuel cell, how does the fuel produce a potential difference?

options.text: It is oxidised electrochemically at an electrode
It is burned, and the heat drives a generator
It is reduced by oxygen at the negative electrode
It is decomposed by a current supplied to the cell

items.why: The fuel is oxidised electrochemically within the fuel cell to produce a potential difference.

items.stem: Which equation represents the overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell?

options.text: H2 + O2 → H2O + O
H2 + O2 → 2H2O

items.why: The overall reaction is the oxidation of hydrogen to produce water, balanced as 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O.

items.stem: Why are hydrogen fuel cells described as a potential alternative to rechargeable cells and batteries?

options.text: They can be refilled with electricity at any charge point
They store far more electricity inside them than a battery
They need no fuel or oxygen once they have been started
They keep working while hydrogen is supplied, with no recharging

items.why: A fuel cell runs on an external fuel supply, so it does not have to be taken out of use to recharge.

items.stem: A car maker compares a hydrogen fuel cell car with a rechargeable battery car. Which is a genuine disadvantage of the fuel cell car?

options.text: It gives out carbon dioxide as it is driven
Hydrogen is difficult to store safely
It must be plugged in and recharged often
It stops once its battery has gone flat

items.why: Hydrogen is a flammable gas that must be stored under pressure or at very low temperature, which is a real drawback.

items.stem: (HT) A hydrogen fuel cell has an acidic electrolyte. Which half equation shows the reaction at the negative electrode?
items.why: Hydrogen is oxidised at the negative electrode, losing electrons: H2 → 2H+ + 2e−.

items.stem: (HT) A hydrogen fuel cell has an acidic electrolyte. Which half equation shows the reaction at the positive electrode?
items.why: Oxygen is reduced at the positive electrode, gaining electrons: O2 + 4H+ + 4e− → 2H2O.

items.stem: A games controller is used every day and flattens its cells within a week. Which is the best reason for choosing rechargeable cells for it?

options.text: They can be reused many times, so fewer cells are bought
Recharging pushes new chemicals in, so they never wear out
They hold much more electricity inside them when new
They cost less to buy than an alkaline cell does

items.why: With heavy daily use the cost and waste of replacing cells each week outweigh the higher purchase price of a rechargeable cell.
